questions.question: Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i>-1$, with discount factor $v=(1+i)^{-1}$, discount rate $d=1-v$ and force of interest $\delta=\log(1+i)$ ($\log$ natural), which description fits the discount rate $d$?
options: The interest paid at the end of a year on $1$ invested at its start
The interest paid at the start of a year on a loan of $1$ repayable at its end
The instantaneous rate at which an invested amount grows
The amount that must be invested now to receive $1$ in one year

questions.question: Consider compound interest at annual effective rate $i>-1$, with discount factor $v=(1+i)^{-1}$, discount rate $d=1-v$ and force of interest $\delta=\log(1+i)$ ($\log$ natural), at the negative rate $i=-0.02$. Which statement about $v$, $d$ and $\delta$ is correct?
options: $v<1$, because discounting always lowers a later payment's value
The quantities are undefined, because they require $i>0$
$v>1$, but $d>0$ because $d$ is interest paid in advance

questions.question: Money accumulates with a force of interest $\delta(s)$ that varies with time $s\ge0$. Which expression gives the discount factor from time $t$ back to time $0$?
Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i>0$, with $v=(1+i)^{-1}$ and $\delta=\log(1+i)$, which is the effective interest rate for a half-year?
Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i=0.25$, with $v=(1+i)^{-1}$ and discount rate $d=1-v$, what is the difference $i-d$?
Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i=0.05$, with $v=(1+i)^{-1}$, what is the present value at time $0$ of a payment of $200$ due at time $3$ (to two decimals)?
Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i=0.05$, the force of interest is $\delta=\log(1+i)$ with $\log$ the natural logarithm. What is $\delta$ (to six decimals)?

A lender charges interest in advance at annual effective discount rate $d=0.06$: for a loan repayable as $1$ after one year, the borrower receives $1-d$ now. What is the equivalent annual effective interest rate $i$ (to six decimals)?

For annual effective rate $i>0$, the nominal rates $i^{(m)}=m\big((1+i)^{1/m}-1\big)$ and $d^{(m)}=m\big(1-(1+i)^{-1/m}\big)$ describe the same basis with $m$ periods a year; $\delta=\log(1+i)$. What happens as $m\to\infty$?

For annual effective rate $i>0$ and an integer $m>1$, let $d$ be the discount rate, $\delta=\log(1+i)$ the force of interest, and $i^{(m)}$, $d^{(m)}$ the equivalent nominal interest and discount rates. Which ordering holds?
Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i>0$, $1$ invested at time $0$ grows to $A(t)=(1+i)^t$. What is the relative growth rate $A'(t)/A(t)$?
Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i=0.06$ with $v=(1+i)^{-1}$, the nominal discount rate payable quarterly is $d^{(4)}=4\big(1-v^{1/4}\big)$. What is $d^{(4)}$ (to six decimals)?
Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i=0.10$, with $v=(1+i)^{-1}$, a contract pays $110$ at time $1$ and $121$ at time $2$. What is its present value at time $0$?
A deposit earns a nominal rate $i^{(12)}=0.12$ convertible monthly, i.e. $0.01$ per month compounded. What is the equivalent annual effective interest rate $i$ (to six decimals)?

Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i>-1$, with discount factor $v=(1+i)^{-1}$, discount rate $d=1-v$ and force of interest $\delta=\log(1+i)$ ($\log$ natural), suppose the rate is negative, $-1<i<0$. How are the discount rate $d$, the force $\delta$ and $i$ ordered?
options: $d<\delta<i$, the same order as for positive rates
$i<\delta<d$, the reverse of the order for positive rates
$\delta<d<i$, with the force now the smallest

questions.question: Let $i>0$ and $v=(1+i)^{-1}$. A discounting rule assigns the factor $f(t)$ to a payment due at time $t\ge0$. Which rule satisfies $f(t+s)=f(t)f(s)$ for all real $t,s\ge0$, so that discounting in two stages gives the same value as discounting in one?
Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i=0.05$, with $v=(1+i)^{-1}$ and $d=1-v$, what is the present value of payments of $1$ at times $0,1,2,3,4$ (to four decimals)?

An amount of $81$ invested now grows to exactly $100$ after two years under compound interest at a constant annual effective rate $i>0$. At the same rate, how much must be invested now to receive $100$ after half a year (to two decimals)?

Under compound interest at annual effective rate $i>0$, with discount factor $v=(1+i)^{-1}$ and force of interest $\delta=\log(1+i)$ ($\log$ natural), which expression gives the present value at time $0$ of a payment of $1$ due at time $t=2.5$ years?
